```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pfCheck = function(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="margin:18px 0 24px 0;text-align:center;">
    <button style="display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;background:linear-gradient(135deg,#0e7490 0%,#3730a3 100%);color:#fff;border:none;padding:10px 22px;min-height:44px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.95em;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;box-shadow:0 3px 12px rgba(14,116,144,.4);">
      <span style="font-size:1.1em;">📝</span> ${title} <span class="chevron" style="transition:transform .3s;">▼</span>
    </button>
    <div class="quiz-body" style="max-height:0;opacity:0;overflow:hidden;transition:max-height .5s ease,opacity .4s ease,margin-top .3s ease;margin-top:0;text-align:left;">
      <button class="close-btn" style="display:block;margin:0 auto 10px auto;background:rgba(14,116,144,.12);color:#0e7490;border:none;padding:6px 18px;min-height:36px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.85em;font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;">Hide</button>
    </div>
  </div>`;
  const toggle = outer.querySelector("button");
  const chevron = toggle.querySelector(".chevron");
  const body = outer.querySelector(".quiz-body");
  const closeBtn = body.querySelector(".close-btn");
  function expand(){ body.style.maxHeight="4000px"; body.style.opacity="1"; body.style.marginTop="14px"; chevron.style.transform="rotate(180deg)"; }
  function collapse(){ body.style.maxHeight="0"; body.style.opacity="0"; body.style.marginTop="0"; chevron.style.transform="rotate(0)"; }
  toggle.onclick = () => (body.style.maxHeight === "0px" || body.style.maxHeight === "") ? expand() : collapse();
  closeBtn.onclick = collapse;
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 18px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.1);";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;";
    qq.options.forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        card.querySelectorAll("button").forEach(b => b.style.cursor = "default");
        const right = card.querySelectorAll("button")[qq.correct];
        right.style.borderColor = "#48bb78"; right.style.background = "#f0fff4";
        if (oi === qq.correct) {
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#276749"; fb.style.background = "#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor = "#fc8181"; btn.style.background = "#fff5f5";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; fb.style.background = "#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding = "10px 14px"; fb.style.marginTop = "8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  return outer;
}
```

# Engage: How Have Humans Been Impacted by Climate Change in the Past? {#pf-engage}

::: {.engage-box}
## 🌍 We Have Been Here Before

In the last two chapters you figured out **what** causes climate change: orbital factors and the Sun set the slow natural rhythm, and **CO₂ from human activities** is driving the warming today. A fair question is: **so what?** Why is climate change a big deal for people?

One way to find out is to look back. Humans have lived through **ice ages, warm periods, floods, droughts, and huge volcanic eruptions.** Our species survived, but that doesn't mean we came through unharmed.
:::

## Climate and Human Populations {#pf-climate-human-populations}

What the packet reading tells us:

| When | What happened to people | Climate connection |
|---|---|---|
| ~200,000 years ago | Modern humans evolve in Africa | Deserts grew, shrank, and turned to grassland and back; populations moved, grew, and shrank |
| ~120,000 years ago | First wave leaves Africa for the Middle East, then **dies off** | A **drought** caused by global glacial conditions |
| Same era | Population in Africa crashes to perhaps **10,000 mating pairs** | Orbital factors and suspected volcanic activity killed much of the plant life |
| ~60,000 years ago | Second wave leaves Africa across land bridges and **survives** | **Milder temperatures** |
| After that | Humans spread to new continents | Low sea level exposed **land bridges** |

Step through the packet's **Global Journey** map to see when people reached each region.

### The Clovis culture

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pfGisp = [
  [20,-48],[19.5,-47],[19,-48],[18.5,-47],[18,-48.5],[17.5,-46],[17,-47],[16.5,-45.5],[16,-46.5],[15.5,-45],[15,-46],[14.8,-45],
  [14.65,-36],[14.5,-33],[14.3,-35],[14.0,-37],[13.7,-36],[13.4,-38.5],[13.1,-38],[12.9,-42],[12.8,-47],[12.6,-49],[12.4,-50],[12.2,-49.5],[12.0,-50],[11.8,-48.5],
  [11.7,-41],[11.6,-35],[11.4,-33],[11.0,-34],[10.5,-31.5],[10.0,-31],[9.5,-30.5],[9.0,-30.5],[8.4,-31],[8.2,-32.5],[8.0,-31],[7.0,-30.2],[6.0,-30.5],[5.0,-30.4],[4.0,-30.7],[3.0,-31],[2.0,-31.2],[1.0,-31.4],[0.5,-31.8],[0.095,-31.6]
].map(([ka, t]) => ({ka, t}))
```

The packet reading continues: the **Clovis culture**, one of the earliest populations in North America, likely crossed the Bering Land Bridge from Siberia **15,000–20,000 years ago**. Their stone spear points appear across North America starting **13,500 years ago**, and then they **disappear from the record 12,750 years ago**. Many hypotheses exist, but their disappearance happened **at the same time as major changes to the climate.**

The packet's graph is a temperature record from the **GISP2 ice core** at the top of the Greenland ice sheet (Alley, 2000). Toggle the layers to compare the climate with the Clovis timeline.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pfGispShow = Inputs.checkbox(["Bølling–Allerød warm period", "Younger Dryas cold period", "Clovis culture (13,500–12,750 years ago)"],
  {label: "Show:", value: ["Clovis culture (13,500–12,750 years ago)"]})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const bands = [];
  if (pfGispShow.includes("Bølling–Allerød warm period")) bands.push({x1: 14.7, x2: 12.9, fill: "#fca5a5", label: "Bølling–Allerød"});
  if (pfGispShow.includes("Younger Dryas cold period")) bands.push({x1: 12.9, x2: 11.7, fill: "#93c5fd", label: "Younger Dryas"});
  const clovis = pfGispShow.includes("Clovis culture (13,500–12,750 years ago)");
  return Plot.plot({
    title: "Greenland temperature as Earth left the last glacial period",
    subtitle: "GISP2 ice core (Alley 2000); values read from the packet's graph, approximate",
    width, height: 330, marginLeft: 50, marginBottom: 42,
    x: {label: "Thousands of years ago →", domain: [20, 0], reverse: false},
    y: {label: "Temperature (°C)", domain: [-55, -25], grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.rectX(bands, {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -55, y2: -25, fill: "fill", fillOpacity: 0.35}),
      Plot.text(bands, {x: d => (d.x1 + d.x2) / 2, y: -26.5, text: "label", fontSize: 11, fontWeight: "bold"}),
      ...(clovis ? [
        Plot.link([{x1: 13.5, x2: 12.75}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -53, y2: -53, stroke: "#b45309", strokeWidth: 7}),
        Plot.text([{x: 13.1}], {x: "x", y: -51, text: () => "Clovis", fill: "#b45309", fontWeight: "bold", fontSize: 12})
      ] : []),
      Plot.line(pfGisp, {x: "ka", y: "t", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot([{ka: 0.095, t: -31.6}], {x: "ka", y: "t", r: 4, fill: "#0e7490"}),
      Plot.text([{ka: 0.4, t: -33.5}], {x: "ka", y: "t", text: () => "1855", fontSize: 11, textAnchor: "end"}),
      Plot.ruleY([-30], {stroke: "#94a3b8", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
      Plot.tip(pfGisp, Plot.pointerX({x: "ka", y: "t", title: d => `${d.ka} thousand years ago: about ${d.t} °C`}))
    ]
  });
}
```

::: {.pf-note}
The full packet graph goes back 50,000 years and also shows rapid swings called **Dansgaard–Oeschger cycles** during the ice age. The **Holocene** (the last ~11,700 years) has been unusually stable, and it is the only climate in which farming and cities have existed.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pfCheck("pf-check-gisp", "Check: Reading the ice core graph", [
  {q: "Around 14,700 years ago, Greenland temperature jumped from about −46 °C to about −33 °C. Then, at 12,900 years ago, it fell back to about −49 °C. What happened at the same time as the cold drop?",
   options: ["Humans first left Africa", "The Clovis culture disappeared from the record", "The Holocene began", "The Bering Land Bridge formed"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "The Clovis record ends 12,750 years ago, right as the Younger Dryas cold period begins. That's a correlation. Whether the climate caused it is what this chapter investigates."},
  {q: "How fast did Greenland warm at the END of the Younger Dryas (~11,700 years ago)?",
   options: ["About 15 °C over tens of thousands of years", "About 15 °C in a very short time, centuries or less", "It didn't warm; it kept cooling", "About 1 °C"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "On the graph the line jumps from about −49 °C to about −34 °C almost straight up. Ice-core studies show most of that warming took only decades. Orbital changes are far too slow to explain that, so something faster must be involved."},
  {q: "The temperature was rising ~15,000 years ago as Earth came out of the glacial period. Based on Unit 4 so far, what is the most likely cause of that long rise?",
   options: ["Orbital factors increasing summer sunlight in the north, amplified by feedbacks (CO₂ and melting ice)", "Factories", "A volcanic eruption", "The Clovis people"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "This is what you figured out in Earth-Sun Dynamics and Climate Feedbacks. The puzzle is the sudden drop and rebound in the middle."}
])
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Climate and Human Populations

Read the text and study the map and the temperature graph, then think about:

- **How have humans been impacted by climate change in the past?**
- **What changes in temperature do you see on the graph?**
- **What causes can you think of for the changes you see in the graph?**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- Around **15,000 years ago** the climate is **warming**, probably because of **orbital factors** (with feedbacks).
- Suddenly, around **13,000 years ago**, temperatures **drop** (the **Younger Dryas**).
- Then, around **11,500 years ago**, temperatures **rise again**, very quickly.
- During that time, the **Clovis population disappeared**.
- Coming out of a glacial period, **ice should be melting**. So why would temperatures suddenly plunge and then shoot back up? To find out, we need to look closely at **what happens when ice melts**.
:::

# Explore 1: What Impact Does Melting or Freezing Ice Have on Ocean Currents? {#pf-explore1}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🧊 Where Does All That Meltwater Go?

Ice sheets are made of **fresh water**. When they melt, the water flows into the ocean. Two big questions:

1. What happens to **sea level**?
2. What happens to the **salt concentration** of the ocean, and to the **ocean currents** that depend on it?
:::

## Part 1. Sea Level {#pf-sea-level}

Watch **The Blue Marble** video up to **1:36**. Look for similarities between Earth coming out of the last ice age and the climate change happening now.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const interp = ka => {
    for (let i = 0; i < pfSea.length - 1; i++) {
      const a = pfSea[i], b = pfSea[i + 1];
      if (ka <= a.ka && ka >= b.ka) return a.m + (b.m - a.m) * (a.ka - ka) / (a.ka - b.ka);
    }
    return ka > 22 ? -125 : 0;
  };
  const m = interp(pfSeaKa);
  const gone = pfIceZones.filter(z => pfSeaKa <= z.to);
  const melting = pfIceZones.filter(z => pfSeaKa < z.from && pfSeaKa > z.to);
  const chart = Plot.plot({
    title: "Post-glacial sea level rise",
    subtitle: "Sea level compared to today (m); curve read from the packet's graph, approximate",
    width, height: 300, marginLeft: 50, marginBottom: 42,
    x: {label: "Thousands of years ago →", domain: [22, 0]},

    marks: [
      Plot.rectX([{x1: 14.7, x2: 14.3}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", y1: -135, y2: 5, fill: "#f59e0b", fillOpacity: 0.25}),
      Plot.text([{x: 14.5}], {x: "x", y: -128, text: () => "Meltwater Pulse 1A", fontSize: 11, fill: "#b45309", fontWeight: "bold"}),
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.line(pfSea, {x: "ka", y: "m", stroke: "#0b5394", strokeWidth: 2.5, curve: "monotone-x"}),
      Plot.ruleX([pfSeaKa], {stroke: "#e11d48", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.dot([{ka: pfSeaKa, m}], {x: "ka", y: "m", r: 7, fill: "#e11d48", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  });
  return html`<div>${chart}
    <div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:10px;justify-content:center;margin:8px 0;">
      <div style="background:#e0f2fe;color:#0c4a6e;border-radius:10px;padding:10px 14px;min-width:150px;text-align:center;"><div style="font-size:.8em;">Sea level vs. today</div><div style="font-size:1.6em;font-weight:800;">${Math.round(m)} m</div></div>
      <div style="background:#f1f5f9;color:#0f172a;border-radius:10px;padding:10px 14px;max-width:420px;font-size:.9em;">
        <strong>North American ice sheet at ${pfSeaKa} ka:</strong><br>
        ${pfSeaKa >= 18 ? "Near its greatest size, covering most of Canada and the northern U.S." :
          gone.length === pfIceZones.length ? "Gone (except small mountain glaciers)." :
          `Already ice-free: ${gone.length ? gone.map(z => z.zone.split(":")[0]).join(", ") : "none yet"}.` + (melting.length ? `<br>Melting now: ${melting[0].zone}` : "")}
      </div>
    </div></div>`;
}
```

### ✏️ In your packet: Part 1 questions

1. How did **glacial levels** change over the past 20,000 years?
2. How did **sea level** change over the past 20,000 years?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

1. About 20,000 years ago, a huge ice sheet covered most of Canada and the northern U.S. It **melted from the south and west edges inward**: 15–18 thousand years ago at the southern edge, and the last remnants were gone about **5–7 thousand years ago**.
2. Sea level **rose about 120 m**, from roughly −120 m to today's level. The rise was fastest during **Meltwater Pulse 1A (~14,500 years ago)** and leveled off around 6,000–7,000 years ago.
3. **Where did the meltwater go?** Into the ocean, raising sea level. But that water is **fresh**, which brings up the next question: what does fresh water do to the **salt concentration** and the **currents** of the ocean?
:::

## Part 2. Ocean Circulation {#pf-ocean-circulation}

You'll be investigating how melting Arctic ice affects one specific current: the **Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC)**. It carries warm water north on the surface and **sinks toward the bottom of the ocean near Greenland**.

What you already know from middle school:

- **Cold** water sinks; **warm** water rises.
- **Saltier** water is **denser** than less salty water.
- Warm water comes from the **equator**; cold water comes from the **poles**.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🎬 Need a refresher? Watch the AMOC Model video

<div class="pf-video"><iframe src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/eZzpvLz4yAk" title="The Atlantic Meridional Overturning video" loading="lazy" allow="accelerometer; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture" allowfullscreen></iframe></div>
:::

### Plan for setting up the global ocean circulation model

In class, the model is a clear tank of water. One end is the **equator (0°)** and the other end is the **North Pole (90° N)**:

- At the equator end, pour **hot water dyed red**.
- At the North Pole end, pour **cold, very salty water dyed blue** (about 400 g of salt per liter).

**Brainstorm:** Glacial water is **fresh water**. To show glacial melt entering the ocean at the North Pole, make the cold water **less salty** by mixing it with fresh water (1 part salt water to 1, 2, or 3 parts fresh water).

### Make a prediction

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pfPredict = Inputs.radio(["Speed up", "Slow down", "Stay the same", "Reverse direction"],
  {label: "When you add glacial melt (less salty cold water), the current will:"})
```

### Run the virtual models

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pfDilution = Inputs.radio(new Map([
  ["1 : 1 (salt water : fresh water)", 1],
  ["1 : 2", 2],
  ["1 : 3", 3],
  ["All fresh water (the ice keeps melting)", 99]
]), {label: "\"After\" model: how much glacial melt?", value: 1})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof pfRun = Inputs.button("▶ Run both models")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pfTank = {
  pfRun;
  // Densities (g/mL): room-temperature tank water ≈ 0.998; cold brine (~400 g/L) ≈ 1.20.
  const ambient = 0.998, brine = 1.20, fresh = 1.000;
  const coldAfter = pfDilution === 99 ? fresh : (brine + pfDilution * fresh) / (1 + pfDilution);
  const dBefore = brine - ambient, dAfter = Math.max(coldAfter - ambient, 0.0005);
  const tBefore = 3; // seconds for the plume to reach the bottom in the "before" model
  const tAfter = Math.min(tBefore * dBefore / dAfter, 120);
  const uid = "pft" + Math.floor(Math.random() * 1e9);
  const tank = (label, dur, coldColor, note) => {
    const flow = Math.max(dur * 1.6, 1.5);
    return `<div style="flex:1 1 280px;max-width:420px;">
      <div style="font-weight:700;text-align:center;margin-bottom:4px;">${label}</div>
      <svg viewBox="0 0 320 190" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;" role="img" aria-label="${label} tank model">
        <rect x="0" y="0" width="320" height="190" rx="12" fill="#f8fafc"/>
        <path d="M20,30 L300,30 L285,170 L35,170 Z" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2"/>
        <text x="40" y="22" font-size="11" fill="#0f172a">Equator 0°</text>
        <text x="225" y="22" font-size="11" fill="#0f172a">North Pole 90° N</text>
        <rect x="24" y="32" width="120" height="14" fill="#ef4444" opacity=".85" class="${uid}-warm" style="animation:${uid}-spread ${flow}s ease-out forwards; transform-origin:24px 39px;"/>
        <rect x="262" y="32" width="24" height="0" fill="${coldColor}" class="${uid}-sink" style="animation:${uid}-sink-${label.length} ${dur}s ease-in forwards;"/>
        <rect x="140" y="152" width="146" height="16" fill="${coldColor}" opacity="0" style="animation:${uid}-floor ${flow}s ease-out ${dur}s forwards; transform-origin:286px 160px;"/>
        <path d="M60,60 C120,60 200,60 250,60" stroke="#b91c1c" stroke-width="3" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="8 8" style="animation:${uid}-dash ${Math.max(dur, 1) * 0.8}s linear infinite;" marker-end="url(#${uid}-arrR)"/>
        <path d="M255,140 C200,140 120,140 70,140" stroke="#1d4ed8" stroke-width="3" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="8 8" style="animation:${uid}-dash ${Math.max(dur, 1) * 0.8}s linear infinite;" marker-end="url(#${uid}-arrB)"/>
        <defs>
          <marker id="${uid}-arrR" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#b91c1c"/></marker>
          <marker id="${uid}-arrB" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="5" markerHeight="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#1d4ed8"/></marker>
        </defs>
      </svg>
      <div style="font-size:.85em;text-align:center;color:inherit;">${note}</div>
      <style>
        @keyframes ${uid}-sink-${label.length} { from { height: 0; } to { height: 136px; } }
      </style>
    </div>`;
  };
  const speedPct = Math.round(100 * dAfter / dBefore);
  const div = html`<div>
    <style>
      @keyframes ${uid}-spread { from { transform: scaleX(.2); } to { transform: scaleX(1.9); } }
      @keyframes ${uid}-floor { from { opacity: .9; transform: scaleX(.1); } to { opacity: .9; transform: scaleX(1); } }
      @keyframes ${uid}-dash { to { stroke-dashoffset: -32; } }
    </style>
    <div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:14px;justify-content:center;background:rgba(148,163,184,.08);border-radius:12px;padding:10px;">
      ${tank("Before glacial melt", tBefore, "#1e3a8a", `Cold, very salty water (≈1.20 g/mL) sinks in about ${tBefore} s`)}
      ${tank("After glacial melt", tAfter, "#7c3aed", pfDilution === 99 ? "Cold fresh water (≈1.000 g/mL) barely sinks: the current almost stops" : `Diluted cold water (≈${coldAfter.toFixed(2)} g/mL) sinks in about ${Math.round(tAfter)} s`)}
    </div>
    <table class="pf-table" style="max-width:520px;margin:10px auto;">
      <tr><th></th><th>Before</th><th>After</th></tr>
      <tr><td>Density of the cold "polar" water</td><td>≈1.20 g/mL</td><td>≈${coldAfter.toFixed(3)} g/mL</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Extra density vs. tank water</td><td>${dBefore.toFixed(3)}</td><td>${dAfter.toFixed(3)}</td></tr>
      <tr><td>Relative sinking (current) speed</td><td>100%</td><td><strong>${speedPct}%</strong></td></tr>
    </table>
    <p class="pf-note" style="text-align:center;">Simplified model: sinking speed is set in proportion to how much denser the cold water is than the tank water. Real tanks also mix and warm, so times will differ.</p>
  </div>`;
  return div;
}
```

```{ojs}
  You predicted the current would <strong>${pfPredict.toLowerCase()}</strong>. ${pfPredict === "Slow down" ? "✅ Your prediction matches the model: less salty water is less dense, so it sinks more slowly and the whole loop slows." : "The model shows the current <strong>slows down</strong>. Fresher water is less dense, so it sinks more slowly, and the sinking is what pulls the whole loop along. Revise your prediction using this evidence."}
</div>` : html`<p class="pf-note" style="text-align:center;">Choose a prediction, then press Run to compare.</p>`
```

```{ojs}
  {q: "In the \"before\" model, what makes the cold blue water sink at the North Pole end?",
   options: ["It is colder and saltier, so it is denser than the water around it", "It is warmer", "The food coloring is heavy", "Wind pushes it down"],

  {q: "Switch the \"after\" model to all fresh water. What would happen to the AMOC if glaciers kept melting and diluting the North Atlantic?",

])
```

## Making Sense of the Melting Ice Investigation {#pf-making-sense-1}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: See-Think-Wonder + Identify and Interpret

| See | Think | Wonder |
|---|---|---|
| What did you notice about the relationship between **glacier size and sea level**? | How do you think these changes would have impacted **people living in the changing areas**? | What questions do you have? |
| When you **reduced the salt concentration** to model glaciers melting, how did the currents change? | What do you think would happen to the current if glaciers **kept melting** and diluting the salt concentration? | |

1. How do changes in the **cryosphere** (ice) induce changes in the **hydrosphere** (water)?
2. How is **energy moving** in this system, before and after the glacier melts? Where is the energy coming from, in the model and in the oceans?
3. How would ocean currents **slowing** because of melting glaciers affect the amount of **energy** carried from the equator to the Northern Hemisphere?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **See:** As glaciers shrank, sea level rose (about 120 m). With less salt, the cold water sank **more slowly** and the current took longer to form and moved more slowly. With more salt, it formed faster.
- **Think:** Rising seas would have **flooded coastlines and land bridges** where people lived. If melting continued, the current could **keep slowing or even stop**.
- **Wonder:** *What did this mean for climate in the past? What does it mean for our climate in the future?*

1. **Cryosphere → hydrosphere:** Melting ice adds **fresh water** to the ocean. That **raises sea level** and **lowers the salt concentration** near the ice, which makes the water **less dense** and changes how it sinks and circulates.
2. **Energy:** In the model, energy comes from the **hot water** (heated on a stove or in a kettle). In the ocean, it comes from **sunlight absorbed near the equator**. The current carries that warm water **toward the pole**, where it gives off heat, cools, and sinks. After the melt, the loop is slower, so **less energy is moved**.
3. A slower AMOC carries **less heat from the equator to the Northern Hemisphere**, so the north should **cool**.
:::

# Explain 1: How Do Changing Ocean Currents Impact Earth's Climate System? {#pf-explain1}

::: {.explain-box}
## 🔄 From Melting Ice to a Sudden Freeze

Now use your evidence to build a **mechanism**: how could melting ice change ocean currents, and how could that have caused the **sudden cooling (the Younger Dryas)** while Earth was coming out of its last glacial period?
:::

## Part 1: Develop a Model for How Changes in Ocean Currents Occur {#pf-model-currents}

Your model should use **density, sinking, and rising**, and show how currents **move energy** and **over what timeframe**. Here is the chain of cause and effect the evidence supports:

<div class="pf-chain">
  <div class="hot">☀️ Sunlight warms surface water near the <strong>equator</strong>.</div><span class="arrow">↓</span>
  <div class="hot">🌊 The AMOC carries warm, salty surface water <strong>north</strong> (the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Current). It gives off heat to the air on the way.</div><span class="arrow">↓</span>
  <div class="cold">❄️ Near Greenland, the water has cooled and is very <strong>salty</strong>, so it is <strong>dense</strong> and <strong>sinks</strong>.</div><span class="arrow">↓</span>
  <div class="cold">⬅️ Deep cold water flows back <strong>south</strong>; more warm water is pulled north to replace it. The loop takes roughly <strong>a thousand years</strong> for water to travel all the way around the global "conveyor belt."</div><span class="arrow">↓</span>
  <div>🧊 <strong>Change:</strong> Melting ice sheets pour <strong>fresh water</strong> into the North Atlantic → lower salt concentration → <strong>less dense</strong> → <strong>less sinking</strong> → the AMOC <strong>slows or stops</strong> within <strong>years to decades</strong>.</div>
</div>

As the ice sheet melted, huge lakes of meltwater formed at its edge. The biggest, **glacial Lake Agassiz**, was larger than all the Great Lakes combined. A leading hypothesis is that a massive release of its fresh water into the North Atlantic (or the Arctic) slowed the AMOC and triggered the Younger Dryas.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}

### Ocean Heat Storage and Transfer

::: {.key-idea}
From the packet reading:

- **Water has a high heat capacity:** it can absorb and store large amounts of heat without a big rise in temperature.
- Warm currents like the **Gulf Stream** transfer heat to the air and land through **convection and conduction**. The warm water warms the air above it, creating **milder climates** along the coasts it passes.
- This is especially noticeable in **western Europe**, which is warmer than places at similar latitudes.
- **Cold currents** do the opposite: they cool the air and lead to cooler land temperatures.

**Extra detail:** Heat always moves from **hotter to colder**. Water is a poor conductor, so most heat moves into the air by **convection and evaporation**: the most energetic water molecules evaporate, carry energy into the air, and release it when they condense.
:::

Compare places at about the same latitude. The ocean next to them makes a huge difference.

### Modeling How Ocean Currents Affect Climate

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: See-Think-Wonder + model

| See | Think |
|---|---|
| What patterns do you notice about the movement of **warm currents**? | How do you think that movement impacts the climate? |
| What patterns do you notice about the movement of **cold currents**? | How do you think that movement impacts the climate? |

Then **develop a model that shows how a change in ocean currents can affect air temperature (climate).**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your model (try it first!)

A strong model shows:

- **Warm currents** move from the equator toward the poles (mostly along east coasts) and **warm the air** above them. **Cold currents** move toward the equator (mostly along west coasts) and **cool the air**.
- **Ocean currents transport energy from the Sun**, absorbed by the ocean in the tropics, to other places around the globe.
- The **AMOC** carries warm water north, where it cools, becomes saltier and denser, and sinks.
- **If melting glaciers add fresh water** where the AMOC sinks, the water becomes less dense, sinking slows, and the AMOC slows. **Less heat reaches the northern latitudes**, so **air temperatures there drop**.
- **Timeframe:** the AMOC can weaken within **years to decades** after a big freshwater pulse. That is fast enough to explain the sudden drop at the start of the Younger Dryas.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pfCardSort = {
  const n = pfCards.length;
  const order = d3.shuffle(d3.range(n));
  let seq = [];
  const wrap = html`<div style="background:rgba(148,163,184,.1);border-radius:14px;padding:12px;">

    <div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;margin-top:12px;">
      <button class="chk" style="min-height:44px;padding:8px 18px;border:none;border-radius:22px;background:#0e7490;color:#fff;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;">Check my order</button>
      <button class="rst" style="min-height:44px;padding:8px 18px;border:2px solid #0e7490;border-radius:22px;background:transparent;color:inherit;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;">Start over</button>
      <button class="ans" style="min-height:44px;padding:8px 18px;border:2px solid #64748b;border-radius:22px;background:transparent;color:inherit;font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;">Show the answer</button>
    </div>
    <div class="fb" style="margin-top:10px;font-size:.92em;"></div>
  </div>`;
  const pile = wrap.querySelector(".pile"), seqEl = wrap.querySelector(".seq"), fb = wrap.querySelector(".fb");
  const cardStyle = "min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:8px 12px;border-radius:10px;border:2px solid #cbd5e1;background:#fff;color:#0f172a;cursor:pointer;font-size:.9em;";
  function render(marks) {
    pile.innerHTML = ""; seqEl.innerHTML = "";
    order.filter(i => !seq.includes(i)).forEach(i => {
      const b = document.createElement("button");
      b.textContent = pfCards[i]; b.style.cssText = cardStyle + "flex:1 1 220px;";
      b.onclick = () => { seq.push(i); fb.innerHTML = ""; render(); };
      pile.appendChild(b);
    });
    seq.forEach((i, k) => {
      const li = document.createElement("li"); li.style.margin = "5px 0";
      const b = document.createElement("button");
      b.textContent = pfCards[i];
      let st = cardStyle + "width:100%;";
      if (marks) st += marks[k] ? "border-color:#16a34a;background:#f0fdf4;" : "border-color:#dc2626;background:#fef2f2;";
      b.style.cssText = st;
      b.onclick = () => { seq = seq.filter(x => x !== i); fb.innerHTML = ""; render(); };
      li.appendChild(b); seqEl.appendChild(li);
    });
    if (!seq.length) seqEl.innerHTML = `<li style="list-style:none;opacity:.7;margin-left:-24px;">No cards yet.</li>`;
  }
  // Cards 13 and 14 (flooding, food supply) may go in either order.
  const okAt = (i, k) => i === k || (k === 12 && i === 13) || (k === 13 && i === 12);
  wrap.querySelector(".chk").onclick = () => {
    if (seq.length < n) { fb.innerHTML = `Place all ${n} cards first (${seq.length} placed).`; return; }
    const marks = seq.map((i, k) => okAt(i, k));
    const right = marks.filter(Boolean).length;
    render(marks);
    fb.innerHTML = right === n
      ? "✅ Perfect sequence! Warming → ice melt → AMOC slows → northern cooling → rapid rewarming → floods and food loss → the Clovis population could not survive."
      : `🟩 ${right} of ${n} cards are in the right spot. Hint: think in four stages: (1) orbital warming and feedbacks, (2) melting ice slows the AMOC and the north cools, (3) heat builds in the south and rushes back north, (4) impacts on people.`;
  };
  wrap.querySelector(".rst").onclick = () => { seq = []; fb.innerHTML = ""; render(); };
  wrap.querySelector(".ans").onclick = () => { seq = d3.range(n); render(seq.map(() => true)); fb.innerHTML = "Here is the packet's sequence. Flooding and food supply can go in either order."; };
  render();
  return wrap;
}
```

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Part 3. Impact on People

1. Arrange **The End of the Clovis Population Cards** to explain how climate factors affected that group of people.
2. Use evidence from this learning sequence and the card sort to answer: **How did changes in climate influence the Clovis population?**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking: the class consensus (try it first!)

- **Ocean currents transport energy** from the Sun, absorbed in the ocean, to different places around the globe.
- The **AMOC** carries warm water north, where it cools and becomes saltier. **Colder, saltier water is denser** than warmer, less salty water, so it sinks.
- **Melting glaciers released fresh water** into the ocean where the AMOC sinks.
- Because salt concentration affects density and how fast water sinks, the **AMOC could have slowed because of melting glaciers**, so **less heat was transported to the northern latitudes**, and air temperatures dropped (the Younger Dryas).
- But **warm air built up in the Southern Hemisphere** and eventually moved north, so temperatures **rose very quickly**.
- The swing from **warm to cold to warm** caused **floods** and **impacted wildlife and food supplies**, contributing to the **loss of the Clovis population**.
- **Cause or correlation?** The timing lines up, and we have a **mechanism** supported by empirical evidence (the tank model, sea level data, ice-core temperatures). Scientists still debate other factors, which is why the packet says "many hypotheses exist."
:::

## Summary Task {#pf-summary-1}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Summary Task

1. How did the use of **models** help you determine the **mechanism** of rapid warming and cooling in the Northern Hemisphere **16,000–12,000 years ago**?
2. Explain how using **empirical evidence** helped you understand the **cause and effect** mechanisms of environmental factors and their impact on human populations.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Summary Task (try it first!)

1. The **tank model** let us change only one thing (salt concentration) and watch the result: less salt → less dense → slower sinking → slower current. The **current and heat model** showed that a slower AMOC means less heat reaches the north. Together they give a **step-by-step mechanism** for the sudden Younger Dryas cooling and the rapid rewarming after it.
2. The **ice-core temperatures**, **sea level curve**, **ice sheet map**, and **archaeological record** are all measured data. They show *when* things happened. The **model** shows *how* one change can cause another. Matching the timing **plus** a tested mechanism is what lets us go beyond "these happened at the same time" (correlation) to a **causal explanation**.
:::

## Forecasting the Future Investigation Part 1 {#pf-forecast-1}

### Predicting Climate Impacts

These are the values from the packet's **Sea Level Change Data Spreadsheet**: global sea level each **May** and **October** from 1993 to 2025, in mm, compared to the 1993 average (satellite measurements).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pfSLraw = [-5.6,7.6,-1.6,12.6,3.9,17.8,3.4,21.6,6.5,23.9,7.6,17.5,8.5,25.5,13.5,30.0,18.5,34.5,19.1,32.3,21.6,36.6,21.9,26.5,27.6,40.0,28.9,43.6,30.8,42.4,34.8,47.4,37.8,53.3,41.3,51.8,37.2,53.9,47.6,65.0,51.9,63.6,51.8,67.7,60.6,78.3,64.8,76.8,64.1,79.3,66.5,83.6,73.7,88.2,76.6,91.6,80.0,95.6,82.3,97.3,89.2,105.1,93.6,104.0,91.6]
pfSL = pfSLraw.map((mm, i) => {
  const year = 1993 + Math.floor(i / 2);
  const month = i % 2 === 0 ? "May" : "October";
  return {year, month, label: `${month} ${year}`, t: year + (i % 2 === 0 ? 4.5 / 12 : 9.5 / 12), mm};
})
pfSeasonal = d3.range(0, pfSL.length - 1, 2).map(i => ({year: pfSL[i].year, may: pfSL[i].mm, oct: pfSL[i + 1].mm, diff: +(pfSL[i + 1].mm - pfSL[i].mm).toFixed(1)}))
pfAvgSeasonal = d3.mean(pfSeasonal, d => d.diff)
pfAnnualRate = (pfSL.at(-1).mm - pfSL[0].mm) / (2025 - 1993)
```

```{ojs}
  </div>`;
}
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ The rate is not staying the same

A straight-line prediction assumes sea level keeps rising at about **3 mm per year**. But NASA reports that the yearly rate has **more than doubled since 1993**, from about **2.1 mm/yr** to about **4.5 mm/yr in 2024**, because melting ice sheets and glaciers and warming water are adding more each year. That's one reason scientists use **climate models** instead of only extending past trends.
:::

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Forecasting the Future Investigation Part 1

1–3. Open the spreadsheet and make a chart of both columns.
4. Describe the **overall trend** in sea level over the 32 years.
5. Describe the **seasonal variation**.
6. Calculate the **average seasonal sea level change** (highlight cells C3 **and** C4 before dragging, or you'll get negative numbers).
7. Average monthly rate of change = average seasonal variation ÷ 7 months.
8. Annual rate of change = (Sea Level May 2025 − Sea Level May 1993) ÷ (2025 − 1993).
9. Predict sea level change over the next **50** and **100** years.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your numbers (try it first!)

- **Trend:** sea level rose steadily, about **97 mm** from 1993 to 2025.
- **Seasonal variation:** every year sea level is higher in October than in May; the average difference is about **14.3 mm**.
- **Monthly rate (packet formula):** 14.27 ÷ 7 ≈ **2 mm/month** during the seasonal rise.
- **Annual rate:** 97.2 mm ÷ 32 yr ≈ **3.0 mm/yr**.
- **Predictions (straight line):** 50 years ≈ **150 mm (about 6 inches)**; 100 years ≈ **300 mm (about 12 inches)**. Because the rate is speeding up, real rise will likely be **more** than this (see the IPCC projections below).
:::

## Forecasting the Future Investigation Part 2 {#pf-forecast-2}

### Observing Climate Impacts

Global averages are important, but climate change is **not the same everywhere**. In the packet, you use the [IPCC WGI Interactive Atlas](https://interactive-atlas.ipcc.ch/) to look at a region you care about under different **warming scenarios**.

**What is a scenario?** Scientists can't know exactly how much fossil fuel people will burn, so they run climate models for several possible futures called **SSPs (Shared Socioeconomic Pathways)**. The first number describes society's path; the second (like 2.6 or 8.5) describes how much extra energy the greenhouse gases trap by 2100 (in W/m²). **Bigger number = more emissions = more warming.**

The explorer below uses the IPCC's **global** results (AR6, 2021). Pick a scenario and a time period.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pfSSP = [
  {ssp: "SSP1-1.9", desc: "Very low emissions: CO₂ cut to net zero around 2050", near: 1.5, mid: 1.6, long: 1.4, lo: 1.0, hi: 1.8, slr50: 0.18, slr100: 0.38, slrLo: 0.28, slrHi: 0.55},
  {ssp: "SSP1-2.6", desc: "Low emissions: CO₂ net zero after 2050", near: 1.5, mid: 1.7, long: 1.8, lo: 1.3, hi: 2.4, slr50: 0.19, slr100: 0.44, slrLo: 0.32, slrHi: 0.62},
```

## Observing Sea Level Rise {#pf-observing-slr}

In the packet you use NASA's [IPCC AR6 Sea Level Projection Tool](https://sealevel.nasa.gov/ipcc-ar6-sea-level-projection-tool) for a U.S. coastal location in **2080**. Here are the **global** projections from the same IPCC report. The curves pass through the IPCC median values for 2050 and 2100; read 2080 off the curve.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
pfSLRcurve = {
  // Quadratic through (2005, 0), (2050, slr50), (2100, slr100); baseline is the 1995–2014 average.
  return pfSSP.map(s => {
    const t1 = 45, t2 = 95;
    const b = (s.slr100 - s.slr50 * t2 / t1) / (t2 * t2 - t1 * t2);
    const a = (s.slr50 - b * t1 * t1) / t1;
    const f = y => { const t = y - 2005; return a * t + b * t * t; };
    return {ssp: s.ssp, f, pts: d3.range(2020, 2101, 5).map(y => ({ssp: s.ssp, year: y, m: f(y)})), s};
  });
}
```

```{ojs}

  const at80 = pfSLRcurve.map(c => ({ssp: c.ssp, year: 2080, m: c.f(2080)}));

    ]
  });
}
```

## Making Sense of the Forecasting the Future Investigation {#pf-making-sense-2}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: See-Think-Wonder + Analysis Questions

| See | Think |
|---|---|
| What did you notice about the relationship between **temperature increase and climate factors**? | How might that impact people living in that area? |
| Were the **rates of change** for each climate factor the same, or did some change more quickly? | |
| What did you notice about the **projected changes in sea level**? | How might that impact people living in that area? |
| What did you notice about the **rate of sea level rise** in each warming scenario? | |

1. Do you think the changes could be **prevented or reversed**? Support your answer with evidence.
2. What **limitations** exist in using data from the past and present to predict the future?
3. If glacial melt and sea level rise continue, what impacts could that have on the **AMOC**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **See:** As temperatures rise, **precipitation patterns, extreme heat, sea ice, and sea level** all change. The bigger the warming, the bigger and **faster** the changes. Some (like heat extremes) change quickly; sea level rises slowly but **keeps accelerating**.
- **Think:** Coastal communities face **flooding and lost land**; others face **heat, drought, or heavy rain**.

1. **Prevent or reverse?** Lower-emission scenarios (SSP1-2.6) clearly produce **less** warming and sea level rise, so a lot of harm **can be prevented**. But some changes, like sea level rise from ice that has already melted and ocean warming, **continue for centuries** and can't be quickly reversed. Whether a change can be reversed depends on **how big it is and how fast it happens**.
2. **Limitations:** Predictions depend on **inputs we can't know for sure**, especially future greenhouse gas emissions. Past trends may not continue at the same rate (sea level rise is speeding up). Models can't capture everything, such as exactly how fast ice sheets might collapse, so projections come with **ranges**.
3. **AMOC:** More fresh water from melting Greenland ice makes the North Atlantic less salty and less dense, so the AMOC could **slow down or even stop**, just as it may have before the Younger Dryas. The IPCC finds the AMOC is **very likely to weaken this century** (with medium confidence it won't collapse abruptly before 2100).
:::

# Explain 2: How Will Melting Ice Impact Populations Around the World? {#pf-explain2}

::: {.explain-box}
## 🏔️ Beyond Rising Seas

Rising sea level is only one way melting ice affects people. The packet's three texts are excerpts from **"How Melting Ice Affects People and the Planet"** by Susan Cosier (NRDC, November 5, 2024). Each one looks at a different icy part of the world.
:::

## Impacts of Melting Ice {#pf-impacts-melting-ice}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Text 1: Glacial Lakes

- In the Himalayas of **Bhutan**, **Thorthormi Lake** is held back by a **rock dam**. It rises **inch by inch** every year as the glacier feeding it melts.
- When a dam like this fails, it causes a **glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF)**. In **1994**, a dam failed near another lake in the same area, and the flood **killed 21 people**.
- Scientists estimate **15 million people** are vulnerable to sudden flooding from glacial lakes.
- Bhutan plans to **relocate nearly 80 families** from high-risk areas, an extreme last-resort adaptation.
- Melting ice also threatens **drinking water**, **agriculture and aquaculture**, coasts (rising seas), and **infrastructure in permafrost zones**.

### Text 2: Mountains

- Alpine glaciers in the **Himalayas, Andes, and East Africa** are melting at unprecedented rates, especially **tropical** glaciers, which don't get the heavy winter snow that rebuilds midlatitude glaciers.
- In **India (2021)**, an ice and rock avalanche from a receding glacier caused a landslide and flood that **killed about 200 people**, destroyed **two hydroelectric dams**, and forced villages to evacuate.
- In Peru's **Cordillera Blanca**, farmers who grew corn, wheat, and potatoes face **hotter, drier** conditions and are switching crops (like sugar snap peas) and relying on **glacial lake meltwater**.
- That has created conflict over **who controls the water**, as irrigation projects and power companies also compete for it. Local communities who depend on the ecosystem "feel the change... most acutely."

### Text 3: The Poles

- **Arctic sea ice** forms later and melts earlier. Less ice means **darker water absorbs more sunlight**, causing more warming and more melting (a **positive feedback**, from Climate Feedbacks).
- Sea ice used to block **waves**. Without it, waves erode the shore: some **Alaska** shorelines are shrinking **more than 3 feet a year**, and several villages have had to **relocate**.
- **Rain-on-snow** events create icy crusts that hurt **reindeer herds** and the people who rely on them. Inuit communities on Alaska's North Slope can no longer rely on **underground ice cellars** to store food.
- The **Bering Sea snow crab** fishery (about **$227 million a year**) **crashed in 2018–2019** and may never recover.
- In **Antarctica**, warming seas melt ice **from below**. West Antarctica's **Thwaites Glacier** is losing stability, which could raise global sea level and affect millions of people.

:::


::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Impacts of Melting Ice (Read-Generate-Sort-Solve)

In class, groups split up the three texts. Working on your own:

1. **Read** all three texts (or the summaries above). Mark ✔ ideas that confirm what you knew, ◯ ideas that answer a question, and **?** ideas you're unsure of.
2. **Generate** a list of ways climate change will affect populations worldwide.
3. **Sort:** star the one idea you think matters most.
4. **Solve:** Answer **How will climate change impact populations?** using specific data and evidence from the investigation and texts.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking: the class consensus (try it first!)

- **Floods are driving communities to relocate**, and not just on coasts (Bhutan's glacial lakes).
- Floods trigger **landslides** in hilly and mountain regions, which cause damage, kill people, and make populations move (India 2021).
- Changes in mountain conditions affect **agriculture and access to food and water** (Peru).
- **Higher waves** cause more coastal damage, shrinking coastlines from both **erosion and rising water** (Alaska).
- Changes in water conditions impact **seafood stocks** (snow crab).
- Globally, people are seeing **many impacts in different parts of life**: homes, food, water, energy, and jobs.
- **Cause vs. correlation:** each text gives a **mechanism** (melting → lake rises → dam fails; less ice → more wave energy → erosion), not just a coincidence in timing.
:::

## Summary Task {#pf-summary-2}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: Summary Task

5. Some climate events are **temporary**, like a seasonal shift in precipitation, and the damage may be reversible. How are the situations you observed here **similar to or different from** those events?
6. How does the **rate of change** in climate factors, combined with our ability to use **data to make predictions**, help communities **adapt and respond**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your Summary Task (try it first!)

5. A seasonal shift comes and goes. Melting glaciers, rising seas, and lost sea ice are **long-term and mostly not reversible** on human timescales: once a glacier is gone or a shoreline erodes, it doesn't come back next season. Like seasonal events, they cause floods and food problems, but they **keep getting worse** as warming continues.
6. Because we can **measure the rate of change** (e.g., about 3 mm/yr of sea level rise and speeding up) and run **models for different scenarios**, communities can **plan ahead**: relocate families before a dam fails (Bhutan), build protections, change crops, or cut emissions. **Faster change gives less time to adapt**, so good predictions matter more.
:::

# Elaborate: How Else Will Climate Change Impact Humans, and How Can We Try to Mitigate It? {#pf-elaborate}

::: {.elaborate-box}
## 🌾 Climate Change on Your Plate

Melting ice isn't the only threat. Heat, drought, floods, and shifting seasons are already affecting the **food supply**, from the farm to the grocery store.
:::

## Managing Other Climate Change Disruptions {#pf-managing-disruptions}

How big could the effect on crops be? A large study that combined many methods (Zhao et al., 2017) estimated how much **global yields** of the four biggest crops drop for **each 1 °C** of global warming, if farmers don't adapt.

```{ojs}

  ].map(d => ({...d, change: +(d.per * pfCropWarm).toFixed(1)}));
  return Plot.plot({
    title: `Estimated change in global crop yield with ${pfCropWarm} °C more warming`,
    subtitle: "Zhao et al. 2017 (PNAS): about −7.4% maize, −6.0% wheat, −3.2% rice, −3.1% soybean per °C, without adaptation",
    width, height: 230, marginLeft: 110, marginRight: 60,
    x: {label: "Change in yield (%)", domain: [-27, 0], grid: true},
    y: {label: null, domain: crops.map(d => d.crop)},

    ]
  });
}
```

1. After the two videos, write your own response: **How is climate change affecting populations, and what actions could be taken to prevent increasing harm?**
2. In class, you'd discuss with your group. On your own, compare your answer with the ideas in the check below.
3. **Reflection:** How would you change your original answer?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Ideas to compare with (try it first!)

**How climate change is affecting populations:**

- **Heat and drought** lower crop yields (maize, wheat, rice, soybeans) and kill livestock; **floods and storms** destroy fields and roads.
- Crops like **coffee, cocoa, and grapes** are sensitive to temperature changes, so the places they can grow are shifting.
- Climate extremes are a major driver of **hunger**: when harvests fail, food prices rise and families who already spend most of their money on food go hungry. Some are forced to **move**.

**Actions to prevent increasing harm:**

- **Mitigation:** cut greenhouse gas emissions (clean energy, less waste) to stay on a lower-warming scenario.
- **Adaptation:** drought- and heat-tolerant crops, better irrigation and water storage, early warning systems, crop insurance, and food aid for regions hit by extremes.
:::

## Human Displacement and Disaster Data {#pf-disaster-data}

::: {.evaluate-box}
Use this checklist (from **The Past and the Future Rubric**) before you turn in your work.

**Your explanation accurately describes how climate change has been and will continue to impact human populations, including:**

- How **rapid climate change has impacted populations in the past** (Younger Dryas, AMOC slowdown, the Clovis population; early migrations out of Africa)
- The **potential impacts on the AMOC** of ongoing climate change (Greenland meltwater → less dense water → weaker AMOC → less heat to the north)
- How climate change has **already impacted people through melting ice** (glacial lake floods, landslides, water conflicts, coastal erosion and relocation, fisheries)
- How climate change has **already affected food supplies** (crop yields, hunger from climate extremes)
- How climate change could continue to affect **displacements and human migration** (sea level rise, floods, disasters)
- **Evidence is linked to the explanation** using scientific reasoning and logic

**Cause and effect:** your answers clearly explain **whether there is a causal link** between **human activities → climate change → impacts on human populations**, not just a correlation.
:::

# Chapter Summary

| Key Concept | Details |
|---|---|
| **Humans and past climate** | Climate shifts drove human migrations, die-offs, and population crashes; low sea level created land bridges (like Beringia) |
| **Clovis culture** | In North America from 13,500 years ago; disappeared 12,750 years ago, at the start of the Younger Dryas |
| **Younger Dryas** | Sudden return to near-glacial cold (12,900–11,700 years ago), then rapid warming of ~15 °C in Greenland, much of it within decades |
| **Ice sheets and sea level** | The North American ice sheet melted from ~18,000 to ~6,000 years ago; sea level rose ~120 m; Meltwater Pulse 1A ≈ 20 m in ~500 years |
| **AMOC** | Warm, salty water flows north, cools, becomes dense, and sinks near Greenland; it carries tropical heat to the North Atlantic |
| **Fresh water and density** | Meltwater lowers salt concentration → less dense → less sinking → weaker AMOC → less heat to the north → cooling |
| **Ocean heat transfer** | Water's high heat capacity stores lots of energy; warm currents warm coastal air (western Europe), cold currents cool it |
| **Today's sea level** | +97 mm from 1993 to 2025 (≈3 mm/yr), with the rate more than doubling since 1993 |
| **SSP scenarios (IPCC AR6)** | 2081–2100 warming best estimates: 1.4 °C (SSP1-1.9), 1.8 (SSP1-2.6), 2.7 (SSP2-4.5), 3.6 (SSP3-7.0), 4.4 (SSP5-8.5) |
| **Sea level by 2100** | Likely 0.28–0.55 m (SSP1-1.9) up to 0.63–1.01 m (SSP5-8.5); up to ~2 m can't be ruled out; keeps rising for centuries |
| **Melting ice impacts** | Glacial lake floods, landslides, water conflicts, coastal erosion, village relocation, fishery collapse |
| **Food** | Each 1 °C lowers global maize, wheat, rice, and soybean yields by ~3–7% without adaptation; extremes drive hunger |
| **Mitigation vs. adaptation** | Mitigation cuts emissions (the cause); adaptation copes with changes already happening |

```{=html}
<script>
(function() {
  var cards = [
    {text: "Humans have never lived through a major, rapid climate change before.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "Humans lived through ice ages, droughts, and the Younger Dryas, when Greenland temperatures dropped and then jumped about 15 °C within decades. Populations migrated, shrank, and some, like the first wave out of Africa and possibly the Clovis culture, did not survive."},
    {text: "About 20,000 years ago, sea level was roughly 120 meters lower than today.", type: "Fact",
     explanation: "So much water was stored in ice sheets that coastlines were far out to sea and land bridges like Beringia were dry land. As the ice melted, sea level rose about 120 m."},
    {text: "Melting ice only matters because it raises sea level.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "Melting ice is fresh water. It lowers the salt concentration and density of the North Atlantic, which can slow the AMOC and change how heat is spread around the planet. It also causes glacial lake floods and landslides, and threatens water supplies."},
    {text: "Adding fresh water to the North Atlantic can slow down the AMOC.", type: "Fact",
     explanation: "Less salty water is less dense, so it sinks more slowly. The sinking is what drives the overturning loop, so the whole current weakens. The tank model shows this, and the IPCC projects the AMOC will very likely weaken this century."},
    {text: "If the AMOC slowed down, the whole planet would instantly freeze into an ice age.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "A slower AMOC moves heat around; it doesn't remove it. The North Atlantic region would cool, while heat builds up in the Southern Hemisphere. Today, greenhouse gases keep warming the planet overall."},
    {text: "Sea level rises by the same amount everywhere on Earth.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "Sea level rise varies by place because of sinking or rising land, ocean currents, and gravity changes as ice sheets shrink. Parts of the U.S. East and Gulf Coasts, including New York City, are projected to see more than the global average."},
    {text: "Choosing a lower-emission scenario makes a real difference to how much warming and sea level rise happen by 2100.", type: "Fact",
     explanation: "Best estimates are about 1.8 °C for SSP1-2.6 vs 4.4 °C for SSP5-8.5, and roughly 0.44 m vs 0.77 m of median global sea level rise by 2100. The physics is the same; the difference is our emissions."},
    {text: "Climate projections are just guesses, so they aren't useful for planning.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "Projections come from physics-based models tested against past climate and present-day measurements. They give ranges because future emissions are uncertain, and communities use them to plan, like Bhutan relocating families below a dangerous glacial lake."}
  ];
  var idx = 0, score = 0, answered = 0, cardAnswered = false;
  function el(id) { return document.getElementById(id); }
  function updateCard() {
    if (idx >= cards.length) {
      ['pfmf-card','pfmf-myth','pfmf-fact','pfmf-feedback','pfmf-next'].forEach(function(i){ el(i).style.display = 'none'; });
      el('pfmf-done').style.display = 'block';
      el('pfmf-final').textContent = score;
      el('pfmf-count').textContent = cards.length;
      return;

    el('pfmf-card').textContent = cards[idx].text;
    el('pfmf-progress').textContent = 'Card ' + (idx + 1) + ' of ' + cards.length;
    el('pfmf-feedback').style.display = 'none';
    el('pfmf-next').style.display = 'none';
    el('pfmf-myth').disabled = false; el('pfmf-fact').disabled = false;
    el('pfmf-myth').style.opacity = '1'; el('pfmf-fact').style.opacity = '1';
    cardAnswered = false;
  }
  window.pfmfAnswer = function(choice) {
    if (cardAnswered) return;
    cardAnswered = true; answered++;
    var card = cards[idx], correct = (choice === card.type);
    if (correct) score++;
    el('pfmf-score').textContent = score; el('pfmf-total').textContent = answered;
    var fb = el('pfmf-feedback');
    fb.style.display = 'block';
    fb.style.background = correct ? 'rgba(5,150,105,0.25)' : 'rgba(225,29,72,0.25)';
    fb.style.border = '1px solid ' + (correct ? '#34d399' : '#fb7185');
    fb.innerHTML = '<strong>' + (correct ? '✅ Correct! ' : '❌ That\'s a ' + card.type + '! ') + '</strong>' + card.explanation;
    el('pfmf-myth').disabled = true; el('pfmf-fact').disabled = true;
    el('pfmf-myth').style.opacity = (choice === 'Myth') ? '1' : '0.5';
    el('pfmf-fact').style.opacity = (choice === 'Fact') ? '1' : '0.5';
    el('pfmf-next').style.display = 'block';
  };
  window.pfmfNext = function() { idx++; updateCard(); };
  window.pfmfRestart = function() {
    idx = 0; score = 0; answered = 0;
    el('pfmf-card').style.display = 'flex';
    el('pfmf-myth').style.display = 'block'; el('pfmf-fact').style.display = 'block';
    el('pfmf-done').style.display = 'none';
    el('pfmf-score').textContent = '0'; el('pfmf-total').textContent = '0';
    updateCard();
  };
  updateCard();
})();
</script>
```

# End-of-Chapter Quiz {#end-of-chapter-quiz}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
function pfFinalQuiz(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="font-family:'Inter',sans-serif; max-width:720px; margin:18px auto;"></div>`;
  const header = html`<div style="background:linear-gradient(135deg,#0e7490 0%,#3730a3 100%);color:#fff;border-radius:14px 14px 0 0;padding:18px 22px;">
    <div style="font-size:1.1em;font-weight:700;">📝 ${title}</div>
    <div style="font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.9;margin-top:4px;">Select an answer for each question. Feedback appears right away.</div>
  </div>`;
  const body = html`<div style="border:1.5px solid #a5f3fc;border-top:none;border-radius:0 0 14px 14px;background:#f0fdff;padding:14px;"></div>`;
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 18px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.08);";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;";
    qq.options.forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        card.querySelectorAll("button").forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; b.style.background = "#f8fafc"; b.style.color = "#475569"; });
        const right = card.querySelectorAll("button")[qq.correct];
        right.style.borderColor = "#48bb78"; right.style.background = "#f0fff4"; right.style.color = "#276749"; right.style.fontWeight = "700";
        if (oi === qq.correct) {
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#276749"; fb.style.background = "#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor = "#fc8181"; btn.style.background = "#fff5f5"; btn.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; btn.style.fontWeight = "700";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; fb.style.background = "#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding = "10px 14px"; fb.style.marginTop = "8px";
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
  outer.appendChild(header);
  outer.appendChild(body);
  return outer;
}
```
